1:
They differ at once over whether the visit may be explained. Henry will not soften it: taking a Philistine to wife at the beginning of his course was in some degree excusable, but joining himself to a harlot was such a profanation of his honour as an Israelite and as a Nazarite that we cannot but blush to read it, and this vile impurity makes the graceful visage of the Nazarite blacker than a coal. He notes that no business of Samson's at Gaza appears, reports the guess that he went to observe the posture of the Philistines, and answers that if so he forgot his errand; the one thin comfort he draws is that it makes one hope there were no such women among the daughters of Israel. Keil states the motive without excusing it, that Samson went in full consciousness of his superiority in strength, and marks a pointed omission, that it is not said here, as of the earlier marriage, that the thing was of the Lord. Gill sees the courage rather than the sin, that it showed boldness after such a slaughter to venture into one of their strongest cities. Ellicott refuses the question altogether: the narrative is brief and detached, and it is useless to ask how he could venture there safely, whether he went in disguise, or what his object was.

The ambush is described from the little the text gives. Gill supposes the news carried by someone who saw him enter and knew him, or by the woman herself. Clarke says they shut up all the avenues, secured the gates and set men in ambush, meaning to attack him as he left the city early in the morning. Ellicott reads it otherwise, that they did not know which house he was in and that the word may mean they went round the city looking for him; their quietness means they made no attack but, thinking him secured, went to rest. Both Keil and Ellicott notice a gap at the same place, the verb for it was told being wanting before the name of the citizens, dropped through a copyist's error though it stands in all the versions.

Why he rose at midnight is variously guessed. Gill offers three possibilities, that he could not lie longer for the conviction of his conscience, or was warned by a dream, or had an impulse on his spirit; and he pictures the gate barred and bolted with the watch perhaps asleep, not expecting him before daylight. Ellicott supposes rather that he had been told of the plot and found the gates unguarded, unless he killed the guards without waking the city. Keil describes him laying hold of the folding wings of the gate and the two posts and tearing them out of the ground with the bar that fastened them. Ellicott presses the verbs, that they mean to grasp and then to tear up, and that the bar held the two valves together; Gaza had several gates, and the smaller one beside the main gate may be meant. Clarke argues backwards from the feat to the scale of the town: though Samson was very strong we do not find he was a giant, so the gates were probably not large, the cities of that age showing poorly beside modern villages.

The hill draws the last comment. Keil says the phrase means only in the direction of Hebron and does not put the mountain before the city or near it. Clarke feels the difficulty more sharply, the Hebron generally understood being some twenty miles off, and offers two ways out, that there were possibly two places of the name, or that the words mean the road to Hebron. Ellicott closes with a curiosity, that in Mohammedan legend Ali uses the gate of Chaibar as a shield, which may be a confused echo of this event.
4:
Henry opens on the folly of it: the burnt child dreads the fire, yet Samson, who has more than a man's strength, comes short of a child's wisdom, for though more than once brought into the highest danger by the love of women he would not take warning, and this third time pays for all. Keil says it without the rhetoric, that after so successful an act he gave himself up once more to his sensual lusts. Who she was they cannot agree. Clarke reports that some think Samson took her to wife and others that he had her as a concubine, holds that she was a Philistine, and observes that however strong his love, she had none for him, since he always matched improperly and was cursed in all his matches. Ellicott denies both points: she was not, as Milton represents, his wife, but, on the authority of Josephus and the fathers, one who played the harlot among the Philistines; nor is it clear, though generally assumed, that she was a Philistine.

The place is as uncertain as the woman. Gill reports that the valley lay half a mile from the brook whence the spies brought their grapes, that it was famous for the best wine, and that Samson retired there for refreshment and pleasure; he cites Jerome for a village of a similar name north of Eleutheropolis. Clarke says the site is not easy to ascertain, quotes the same authorities for a position south of that city, and then turns the question on itself by asking where Eleutheropolis was. Ellicott adds a philological doubt, that the English rendering follows the Vulgate while the Hebrew may equally mean on the brook of Sorek, and that Sorek was not in the Philistine district at all.

On the bribe they are more nearly agreed. Gill counts the lords as five, with five principalities among them, and notes the opinion that men so great did not come to such a house in person. Clarke names the five cities and explains their reasoning, that since Samson's stature was not remarkable while his strength was extraordinary, they supposed some charm. Keil reckons the sum, eleven hundred shekels of silver from each of them, and calls it considerable. Ellicott adds a motive from her character, that if she was what Josephus asserts the Philistines could both reach her and tempt the cupidity of a degraded mind, whereas with a woman of their own race threats would have served better.

The first trial follows, and its strangeness is felt. Ellicott admits that the narrative, taken as a full account of what passed, would leave an impression of almost incredible fatuity on Samson's part, and sets against it the old saying that many have gone out of their wits for women and become slaves on account of them. What the bonds were is disputed. Clarke takes the withs for any pliant tough wood twisted into a cord, such as are made of osiers or hazel, and mentions the strong ropes made in Ireland from bog-wood, though the Greek and Latin versions understood cords of sinews. Ellicott judges them probably right in reading fresh sinews, and dismisses the vine shoots of Josephus as ridiculously inadequate; the seven he takes as the sacred number of perfectness, and finds in it a sign that even thus early Samson is playing about on the confines of his secret. Gill supposes the men in wait to have been servants of the lords placed there privately, whom Josephus calls soldiers, while Ellicott reads the phrase as a single spy sitting in the room to help her, doubting whether there was more than one; he also infers that she bound Samson while he slept. Keil records only that the spy sat in the room for her, and Clarke that the watchers probably never appeared, Samson breaking his bonds the moment she cried out.
10:
Both fill in what the text leaves out about the interval and the pretence. Gill says the second attempt was not made on the same day but some time after, when an opportunity offered, since an immediate return to the question might have created suspicion of the design against him; he cites Kimchi for it. Ellicott supplies the woman's manner: she would of course tell Samson that the scene had been merely a playful jest, and that she raised the alarm only for the pleasure of one fresh exhibition of his strength; her desire to know she would represent as nothing but loving curiosity.

The second answer is read as part of a deliberate game. Clarke says Samson wished to keep up the opinion the Philistines already held, that his strength was the effect of some charm, since the green withs, the new ropes and the number seven are just such matters as would be looked for in a spell. Ellicott makes a different point, that here again Samson distantly touches on the consecration which is the real secret of his strength; and he glosses the old English word in the verse, that occupied means used, citing the gold occupied for the work of the tabernacle and a phrase of Ascham's. Gill reports from Abarbinel a reading that saves Samson's veracity, that he had told her the truth at first and only omitted one circumstance, namely that the cords should be new and never used. Keil counts it the second deception.

The third answer brings him nearer still. Clarke supposes the long hair plaited into seven divisions, and finds a meaning in the number: since the Nazarite vow obliged him to wear his hair, and seven was among the Hebrews a number of perfection, the dividing of it so might point out the perfection designed by that state. Ellicott corrects a familiar picture, that the locks of the Nazarite did not, as Milton imagines, lie waving about his shoulders but were plaited; he notes that the word occurs here only and is rendered curls and plaits in the Greek, that the word for web is technical and perhaps means the warp, and that with almost incredible levity Samson now goes to the very verge of the true secret. Keil gives the same rendering, that the seven locks were to be woven together with the warp.

At this point all of them notice that the text is defective. Clarke says every reader must see that the verse ends abruptly without a full sense, and reports that Houbigant marked the same and corrected the text from the Greek version, which he sets out at length. Gill says that if that addition may be admitted as genuine, supplying what seems wanting and agreeing best with what follows, the whole becomes plain and easy. Ellicott puts the alternative sharply: unless those additions stood in the original text, Samson never told her to drive the pin at all, and she did it of herself to make assurance doubly sure; the versions differ even here, one driving it into the wall and the other into the ground. On the machinery he presses the technical words, that the pin seems to be the peg by which the web was fastened down and the beam is not the weaver's beam of the giant's spear but apparently the comb, the loom being of the simple domestic kind; and the verb rendered went away with is the one used of the gates of Gaza and means tore up. Gill leaves the question open, offering the beam so that it might not roll back, or the loom to the ground so that it might stand firmly, or the web itself with the hair woven into it, and confessing that which is right is difficult to say.
15:
The reproach is the same weapon used a fourth time, and both notice that it should have been recognised. Gill describes the occasion, that she took her opportunity while he was caressing her to upbraid him with dissembled love and a false heart, the three mockeries she counts being the three answers already given. Ellicott puts it more sharply: Samson had undergone all these wiles before and experienced their hollowness, and yet had not learnt wisdom by them.

What broke him at last was not a threat but a repetition. Gill says she lay at him day after day to have the secret communicated, gave him no rest, and was incessant in her applications. Keil says she plagued him every day until his soul became impatient even to death, and notes that the rare verb used here occurs only in this place and is Aramaic for pressing or plaguing. Ellicott renders the phrase literally, that his soul was shortened to death, and makes the weariness the whole reason for the disclosure; but he will not let the excuse stand alone, since even the dangerous use Delilah had made of the last revelation had not roused his mind from its besotted stupefaction. He sets the balance of the story in a sentence: if Samson thrice proved his vast strength, he thrice proved his immense folly, and to spend that strength merely on saving his own life was to squander it, while now, as though possessed by insanity, he trifles with the key of his secret. To the same effect he quotes Milton's lines about a man swollen with pride falling into the snare of fair fallacious looks and laying his head, and the hallowed pledge of all his strength, in the lap of a deceitful woman.

Clarke is harsher still and is willing to name the fault as sin rather than weakness. What a consummate fool, he exclaims, was this strong man; might he not have seen from what had already taken place that Delilah intended his ruin? After trifling with her and lying three times he at last commits to her his fatal secret, and so becomes a traitor both to himself and to his God. He then borrows a judgment from Calmet which sums up the whole chapter, that the weakness of Samson's heart in all this history is yet more astonishing than the strength of his body.

The telling itself is marked as complete. Gill observes that Samson had told her something before, or something nearer the truth, when he directed her to the weaving of his locks, but that now he told her all; and Keil that he opened his mind thoroughly, saying that no razor had come upon his head because he was a Nazarite from his mother's womb, and that if shaven his strength would depart and he would be weak like other men. On what the strength actually depended Clarke gives the explanation the chapter needs. The miraculous strength of Samson, he says, must not be supposed to reside either in his hair or in his muscles, but in that relation in which he stood to God as a Nazarite, such a person being bound by a solemn vow to walk in strict conformity to the laws of his Maker. It was part of that vow to permit no razor to pass upon his head, so that the long hair was the mark of his Nazirate and of his vow to God; and when he permitted it to be shorn off he renounced and broke the vow, in consequence of which God abandoned him, which is why we are told a little later that the Lord was departed from him.
18:
How Delilah knew she had the truth is variously accounted for. Keil says she perceived it from his words and whole behaviour, and Ellicott that she could not mistake the accent of truthfulness, Samson not being so far gone as to reveal the great secret without some sense of awe and shame. Gill collects the Jewish answers, that she read it in his countenance, that Abarbinel conjectures he may have sworn to her, and that the rabbins and Kimchi make the proof his naming of God, a name she knew he would not take in vain. Henry watches the woman rather than the man, noting what care she took to secure the money, the lords being sent for only on condition that they brought the silver.

The shaving is filled out from what the narrative implies. Gill supposes a sleepy potion, or a lulling to sleep by her fondness. Ellicott reasons the same way, that since the locks could hardly have been shorn without waking him from an ordinary sleep, the wording suggests some drowsy syrup; Both he and Keil take the man she called for to be the spy already concealed there, Keil adding that she would not be alone while the hair came off. Clarke supplies the rest, that she had probably tied his hands slyly while he slept, and after cutting the hair insulted him before calling anyone, to try whether he was really weak; only then did she call the Philistines.

On the clause that follows they agree that it is the centre of the chapter. Keil records that Samson thought to go out as at other times and shake himself loose, not knowing that Jehovah had departed. Ellicott calls it a deeply tragic clause, and draws the lesson that men do not know how much they are changed when the Lord departs until they feel it in shame and weakness; Samson was under a vow but too weak to resist the current running counter to it, once he had come to rely on the mere external sign, since his strength was in no sense in his hair but in the dedication it stood for.

The punishment is read as fitted to the sin. Clarke says the lust of the eye, in gazing on strange women, was thus punished, and adds a reason of policy, that since the Philistines did not know his strength might not return they blinded him so that he could never plan anything against them; the grinding he explains from the state of the art, since before wind and water mills grain was ground in hand-mills, as still in the East. Ellicott prefers the margin's bored out, reports the Arabic gloss that the eyes were burnt out with a red-hot style, and observes that blinding was the most effectual humiliation, as the last king of Judah found from the Chaldeans; the fetters he renders literally as two brasses, and Keil explains the dual of both hands and both feet being bound.

The last verse they take as the turn. Gill says the hair began to grow immediately, but probably in an extraordinary manner; and he is careful that the strength did not lie in the hair, since Samson, made sensible of his sin and repenting, renewed his Nazariteship, of which the growing hair was the token. Clarke asks it as a question, whether Samson, sensible of his sin and folly, renewed his vow and had his strength restored in consequence. Henry says that though the last stage of his life was inglorious there was honour in his death, that he greatly repented of the dishonour done to God, and that the returning sign of his Nazariteship proves God reconciled to him; Keil finds the same in the wording, that Samson lay captive only until his hair began visibly to grow.
23:
Gill dates the assembly some time after the capture, perhaps some months, and Keil explains its occasion, that the captivity of so dreaded a hero was reckoned a great victory, celebrated with a joyous sacrificial festival in honour of the god to whom they ascribed it, the greatness of the sacrifice lying in the number of victims. On the god Clarke quotes Diodorus, that it had the head of a woman while the rest of the body resembled a fish, notes that the heathens also called the deity Dorceto, and finds the very image in Horace's lines about a painter who joins a horse's neck to a human head and lets a woman beautiful above end in an ugly black fish. Ellicott describes the same figure as upward man and downward fish, points to the stump left when the fish-part broke off, derives the name from the word for fish and finds the same root in the name of a Spanish river, and reports the parallel goddess Atargatis or Derceto. He measures how widely the worship spread by the commonness of a place-name compounded with the god's, and notes that the chief temple at Azotus was burned in the Maccabean wars.

The songs are noticed by two. Gill says the people praised their god as a later king praised his, in hymns composed for the occasion, and Keil that all took part and sang praises to the god who had given into their hands the enemy who had laid waste their fields and slain many of their countrymen.

What the sport consisted in none of them will say confidently. Gill sets the scene, that they were merry with the wine for which Gaza is famous in many writers, and with eating and dancing and music, since it was usual for the heathen to feast in their temples. Ellicott lists the possibilities and declines to choose, whether by forced jests, or feats of strength, or mere submission to insult; he cites Josephus that they sent for Samson to insult him over their wine, and the Greek version, that he played before them while they beat him with rods. Clarke inclines to feats of strength, as the notice of the restored hair seems to intimate, and observes that the exertion would account for the weariness that gave Samson his pretext for asking to lean against the pillars; but he reports the other view too, and cites the Greek reading that they buffeted him. Henry draws the moral, that nothing fills up the sins of any person or people faster than mocking and misusing the servants of God, even when it is by their own folly that they have been brought low.

The last details are architectural, and the guessing is admitted. Gill remarks only that nothing is commoner now than for a blind man to be led by a boy. Ellicott says the temple had a flat roof but that beyond this we cannot conjecture its architecture, and refers the curious to a study of Gaza; he notes that different words for men and women are used in the two halves of the verse, and infers that the notables were with the lords inside while the common people were on the roof. He offers one reconstruction, a hall like a Turkish kiosk whose roof rested in front on four columns, two at the ends and two close together in the centre. Clarke leaves even the kind of building open, whether prison-house, house of assembly or temple, but agrees that it was raised on pillars, open on all sides and flat-roofed, so that it could carry a multitude on the top. Keil records the request itself, that Samson asked the attendant who held his hand to let him loose and let him touch the pillars on which the house rested.
28:
The prayer raises a question of transmission before one of character. Gill supposes it made mentally, or spoken aloud unheard amid the noise, and if heard would only have furnished ridicule; he draws the consequence that the words must have been preserved by the Lord and given by inspiration to the writer, since none who heard them lived to relate them. Clarke uses the prayer to place Samson in the roll of the faithful, named there for his faith that God would strengthen him against his country's enemies. Ellicott is far less admiring. He counts three names of God in the address, and finds in the petition a proof that Samson stood at a comparatively low level of spiritual enlightenment and of moral purity; he cannot help feeling that Milton read into the character an austere grandeur it did not possess, the Samson of that stern classic poem being rather Milton himself, a mighty spirit struck by the plectrum of disappointment. He adds a rendering of the clause, that Samson asks to avenge the revenge of one of his two eyes.

The two pillars have long drawn an objection, answered in two very different ways. Gill states the difficulty, that a building so large could not be supported by two pillars set so near together that one man could hold both; and he answers by parallels, that the architecture of the ancients is little known and may have had lost arts, that Pliny tells of Curio's two Roman theatres which held far more people and turned on a single hinge, and that Westminster hall may be compared. Clarke thinks the labour wasted: there may have been as many pillars as in the temple of Diana at Ephesus, and yet these two in the centre be the key of the structure, so that once they fell the whole house must fall. Keil describes the act, that Samson embraced the two middle pillars and leaned upon them, one with each hand, and finds no ground for questioning its possibility; Ellicott prefers the marginal rendering, that he leaned himself upon them.

The death is defended rather than reported. Gill says Samson sought their death and was content to lose his own to be avenged, and that in neither did he act a criminal part as a judge of Israel, since from a public spirit he might desire the death of the nation's enemies, the more justified because they were affronting the most high God in the very temple of their idol; his own death he did not desire but was willing to submit to. Keil records that he bent the pillars with force and the house fell on the princes and all within. Clarke reckons the loss: the house was full and some three thousand on the roof, so the principal part were slain, the lords among them, and the crush to the Philistine ascendancy was such that they troubled Israel no more for several years.

The burial closes the chapter. Gill takes those who came down as the kindred of the father's house, but thinks it not unlikely that Samson had brothers in the proper sense, his mother, barren before his birth, having perhaps had many children after. Ellicott supposes Manoah and his wife already dead, and accounts for the unhindered removal by the religious terror the catastrophe caused at Gaza; and he closes, having criticised the poet earlier, by quoting his line that Samson has quit himself like Samson. Keil says the blow necessarily made a powerful impression, plunging the Philistines into mourning for their princes and their temple. Clarke ends on the judgeship, hard to date or measure, the jurisdiction seeming very limited and reaching no further than the parts of Dan next to the Philistines; many suppose Samson and Eli contemporaries, Samson being rather an executor of divine justice on his people's enemies than an administrator of the laws.
